chapters.title: Chapter 6: Using Financial Statements at Work

lessons.title: Building a Business Case Finance Will Approve: Payback, ROI and Breakeven

children.text: Two proposals reach the CFO in the same week. The first says the investment will improve efficiency, strengthen customer experience and position the company for the future. The second says: ₹5 crore, saves ₹1.8 crore a year, pays back in under three years, returns 23% against a 12% hurdle, and still pays back inside four years if savings come in a quarter below plan.

The second one gets funded, and not because the project is better. It gets funded because the CFO can defend it to the board in one sentence. This lesson gives you the four numbers that turn a proposal into a decision.

body.text: Finance does not approve ideas. It approves cash flows with dates attached and a stated downside. Bring the second thing and the idea sells itself.

children.text: A business case measures the difference between two futures: the world with your project and the world without it. Everything that is identical in both drops out.

body.caption: What goes in, what stays out

cells: Only cash that exists because of the decision
Money already spent cannot be recovered by any choice you make now
Extra volume needs extra inventory and receivables
It does not change because of your project, unless it genuinely does
Savings are taxed, and depreciation shields some of it
Depreciation itself, as a cash item
It is non-cash. It matters only through the tax it saves
Land or a team used here cannot be used elsewhere
If nobody will be measured on it, it will not happen
Almost nothing delivers full benefit in year one
The best case as the base case
Plan on the expected case and test the downside separately

body.text: The most expensive mistake in Indian capex proposals is forgetting working capital. A ₹5 crore line that adds ₹20 crore of sales also adds several crore of inventory and receivables, funded from day one and never recovered until the business shrinks. Finance will ask. Have the number ready.

body.title: Which number is irrelevant?
body.question: Kesari Foods has already spent ₹35 lakh on a feasibility study for a new plant. The plant will cost a further ₹5 crore and generate ₹1.8 crore a year. How should the ₹35 lakh be treated in the investment decision?
options: Added to the ₹5 crore, making the investment ₹5.35 crore
Ignored, because it is a sunk cost that cannot be recovered either way
Spread across the project life as an expense
body.explanation: The ₹35 lakh is gone whether or not the plant is built, so it cannot affect the decision. Including it makes a good project look worse and can lead you to reject an investment that would create value from here on.

children.text: Take the Kesari Foods packing line: ₹5 crore of capital expenditure, expected to generate ₹1.8 crore a year of additional cash for five years. The company uses a hurdle rate of 12%.

body.caption: Discounting each year's cash back to today at the hurdle rate

stats.label: Payback
stats.context: How long until the money comes back

stats.label: Net present value at 12%
stats.context: Value created over and above the hurdle

stats.label: Internal rate of return
stats.context: The project's own return, comparable across proposals

stats.label: Accounting return
stats.context: Average annual profit after depreciation and tax, on the ₹5 crore invested

body.title: Cumulative cash flow on the ₹5 crore packing line (₹ crore)

children.text: The line crosses zero partway through year three, which is the payback point. Everything after that is return. Each of the four numbers answers a different question, and a good proposal carries all four.

cells: How long is our money at risk?
Ignores everything after payback, so it favours short projects over valuable ones
How much value does this create in today's rupees?
A large NPV may need a large investment, so it does not show efficiency
What return does the project earn on its own?
Can mislead when cash flows change sign, and it assumes reinvestment at the same rate
What will this do to reported profit and ROCE?
Uses accounting profit rather than cash, so it is distorted by depreciation policy

children.text: A rupee next year is worth less than a rupee today, because today's rupee can be used, invested or used to repay a loan. Discounting simply converts future rupees into today's money so that amounts arriving at different times can be added up.
usually the company's cost of capital, being a blend of what lenders and shareholders require. Many mid-sized Indian companies use something in the 12% to 15% range.
the minimum return a project must clear, often set a little above the cost of capital to allow for optimism in forecasts.
a positive NPV means the project earns more than the hurdle rate, so it creates value. NPV of zero means it earns exactly the hurdle rate, which is acceptable but not exciting.
₹1.8 crore a year for five years discounted at 12% is worth about ₹6.49 crore today. Against a ₹5 crore investment, that is about ₹1.49 crore of value created.
You do not need to compute this by hand. Any spreadsheet does it with NPV and IRR functions. What you must do is state the rate you used and where it came from.

body.title: Work out the payback
body.prompt: A warehouse automation project costs ₹80 lakh and is expected to save ₹25 lakh of cash a year. What is the simple payback period, in years?
body.explanation: ₹80 lakh ÷ ₹25 lakh = 3.2 years. Note that simple payback ignores the timing of cash within the year and everything that happens after year 3.2, so use it as a risk check rather than as the decision.

body.title: The bar to clear
body.textWithBlank: The minimum return a project must earn before a company will approve it is called the ___ rate.
body.explanation: It is usually set at or slightly above the company's cost of capital. A project returning less than the hurdle destroys value even when it reports an accounting profit.

children.text: Every forecast is wrong. The question a CFO is really asking is how wrong it can be before the decision changes. That single table turns a hopeful proposal into a credible one.

body.caption: Kesari packing line: what if the savings disappoint?

body.text: The useful sentence is the last row: this project still creates value as long as it delivers about ₹1.39 crore a year, which is 77% of plan. Saying that out loud shows the board you have thought about being wrong, and it is far more persuasive than defending the forecast.

body.title: Two versions of the same proposal

columns.label: What gets rejected
points: Benefits described as efficiency and customer experience
No working capital, no tax effect
No downside case, so the CFO invents one

columns.label: What gets approved
points: Benefits quantified as annual cash, with the source of each
Capital cost, working capital and the ramp-up profile
Payback, NPV and IRR against the stated hurdle rate
The break-even level of benefit, stated as a percentage of plan
A named owner and a date for a post-implementation review

body.title: Automate the packing line or add a third shift?
body.scenario: Kesari Foods needs 30% more packing capacity. Option A is the ₹5 crore automated line, saving ₹1.8 crore a year in labour and wastage, with a nine-month installation. Option B is a third shift at ₹1.4 crore a year of additional employee and power cost, available in six weeks and reversible. The CFO is protecting cash and the company borrows at about 11%.
body.prompt: Build the comparison and make a recommendation.
body.modelAnswer:
Frame it as three questions: how much capacity, for how long, and how certain is the demand.
The numbers:
1. Option A: ₹5 crore now, then ₹1.8 crore a year of benefit. Payback about 2.8 years, NPV about ₹1.49 crore at a 12% hurdle, IRR about 23%. It clears the hurdle comfortably.
2. Option B: no capital, ₹1.4 crore a year of cost, reversible at short notice. Over five years that is ₹7 crore of cash out against ₹5 crore for the line, but spread and cancellable.
3. Crossover: the automated line is cheaper in cash terms from roughly year four onward, and only if the volume actually persists.
What decides it:
4. Demand certainty. If the 30% is contracted or structural, automate. If it is a festive or a single-customer surge, take the shift, because reversibility is worth real money.
5. Cash and covenants. ₹5 crore now almost certainly means borrowing, which lifts debt to equity from 0.62 to about 0.86 and pushes interest coverage down. The CFO has already said cash is the constraint.
6. Timing. Nine months of installation means the capacity arrives after the season that needs it. A third shift arrives in six weeks.
7. Working capital. Both options raise volume, so both need extra inventory and receivables, roughly ₹10 crore of working capital for every ₹50 crore of sales at current ratios. This is funding neither option includes.
My recommendation:
8. Take the third shift now to meet demand, and run the automated line as a funded proposal for the next financial year, with approval conditional on two quarters of sustained volume.
9. Use the shift period to firm up the savings estimate with real data, so the capex case is built on measured labour and wastage rather than a vendor's brochure.
10. Commit to a post-implementation review twelve months after any automation goes live, comparing actual savings with the ₹1.8 crore claimed.

body.title: Before you send the proposal
steps: State the problem and the do-nothing case in two sentences each.
List every cash flow that changes, including working capital and the tax effect.
Strip out sunk costs and any benefit without a named owner.
Compute payback, NPV and IRR, and say which hurdle rate you used and why.
Add a sensitivity table showing the break-even level of benefit as a percentage of plan.
Name who is accountable for delivering the benefit and set a date for the post-implementation review.

cards.definition: Cash that exists only because the decision is taken. The only cash a business case should count.
Money already spent that cannot be recovered, and which must be excluded from the decision.
The time taken for cumulative cash inflows to recover the investment.
The value created by a project after discounting all future cash flows at the hurdle rate.
The discount rate at which a project's NPV is zero, used to compare proposals.
The minimum acceptable return, usually set at or above the cost of capital.
Testing how far the assumptions can be wrong before the decision changes.
Comparing actual results with the business case after the project is live.

points: A business case compares two futures and counts only the cash that differs between them.
Include working capital, the tax effect and a realistic ramp-up. Exclude sunk costs and unowned synergies.
Payback answers how long the money is at risk, NPV how much value is created, and IRR what the project earns on its own.
A positive NPV means the project beats the hurdle rate. Below the hurdle, a project can report profit and still destroy value.
The strongest slide in any proposal is the break-even level of benefit, stated as a percentage of plan.
Name an owner and book a post-implementation review, or the benefits will never be checked.

body.text: Kesari Foods and the warehouse project are fictional, and the hurdle rate, tax effects and borrowing costs used are illustrative. Real appraisals should use your own company's cost of capital, tax position and approval thresholds.
